title: A Course Correction in Steerability Evaluation: Revealing Miscalibration and Side Effects in LLMs
authors: Trenton Chang, Tobias Schnabel, Adith Swaminathan, Jenna Wiens
finding: Defines steering error in a goal-space and separates along-target miscalibration from orthogonal side effects; strong models still make unintended changes.
experiments: A uniformly sampled text-rewriting probe over reading difficulty, formality, lexical diversity, and length; comparisons of prompts, best-of-N, and RL.
limitation: Single-turn text rewriting, rule-based attributes, and RL on one 8B model in a two-dimensional goal-space.
future: Extend to learned goals, style, multi-turn interaction, higher-dimensional spaces, and side-effect-aware training.

title: What's Producible May Not Be Reachable: Measuring the Steerability of Generative Models
authors: Keyon Vafa, Sarah Bentley, Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan
finding: Separates producibility from reachability: a model may be able to sample a high-quality output that a user cannot reliably elicit for a specific goal.
experiments: Human reproduction studies for text-to-image models and LLMs, with targets sampled from the model itself.
limitation: Human search behavior and interface affordances are entangled with the measured model property.
future: Study adaptive interfaces, target complexity, user heterogeneity, and mechanisms that improve reachability without narrowing output diversity.

title: Evaluating the Prompt Steerability of Large Language Models
finding: Models have baseline personas and limited, directionally asymmetric movement away from them; larger models are usually more prompt-steerable.
experiments: Behavioral profiles and steerability curves across persona dimensions, models, directions, and prompt budgets.
limitation: Measures persona responses rather than downstream actions; the benchmark does not isolate the mechanism causing rigidity.
future: Connect prompt steerability to in-context learning and develop pluralistic systems that do not collapse to an average preference.

title: The Steerability of Large Language Models toward Data-Driven Personas
finding: Data-driven personas capture opinion variation more precisely than coarse demographic labels and improve steering on OpinionQA.
experiments: Individual and clustered persona embeddings across selected LLMs and OpinionQA responses.
limitation: Opinion prediction is only one slice of pluralism and risks treating observed survey responses as stable preferences.
future: Evaluate temporal preference drift, contested values, privacy, and generalization from stated opinions to real decisions.

title: Instruction-Following Evaluation for Large Language Models
finding: Introduces an objective, reproducible instruction-following benchmark with 25 types of verifiable constraints.
experiments: Roughly 500 prompts containing one or more programmatically checkable instructions.
limitation: Verifiability favors surface-form constraints and underrepresents semantic, interactive, or value-laden goals.
future: Preserve evaluator reliability while expanding to semantic constraints, conflicts, and multi-turn instruction revision.

title: FollowBench: A Multi-level Fine-grained Constraints Following Benchmark for Large Language Models
target: Content, situation, style, format, and example constraints
finding: Constraint-following degrades as instructions accumulate; a single quality score hides which individual constraints fail.
experiments: Five constraint families, multiple difficulty levels, and 13 open- and closed-source models.
limitation: Open-ended constraints depend on a strong LLM judge and the benchmark is largely static.
future: Measure interactions among constraints, adversarial compositions, and whether training transfers to unseen constraint structures.

title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
intervention: Prompts, finetuning, SAEs, probes, vectors, ReFT-r1
finding: On its benchmark, prompting is the strongest steering baseline, finetuning is next, and tested SAEs lag simpler representation methods.
experiments: Concept detection and open-ended concept steering on Gemma-2 2B and 9B with standardized data and metrics.
limitation: Synthetic concept tasks, two model sizes from one family, and automatic steering metrics bound external validity.
future: Test causal feature selection, compositional concepts, stronger side-effect metrics, and cross-family transfer.

title: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
finding: Reward models show distinct weaknesses on difficult and out-of-distribution preference pairs, including refusal and reasoning failures.
experiments: Prompt–chosen–rejected trios with verifiable preference rationales and a public leaderboard.
limitation: Pairwise accuracy does not fully predict downstream policy behavior or reward overoptimization.
future: Evaluate calibration, distribution shift, personalization, and causal downstream effects of reward-model errors.

title: Steering Language Models with Activation Engineering
finding: A difference between activations induced by a prompt pair can steer high-level output properties without optimizing model weights.
experiments: Sentiment, topic, detoxification, and qualitative generation across OPT and Llama-family models.
limitation: Direction, layer, token position, and multiplier are behavior- and model-dependent; evaluation of side effects is incomplete.
future: Learn when linear directions compose, how they transfer, and how to select interventions without exhaustive search.

title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
target: Sycophancy, hallucination, refusal, power-seeking, and related behaviors
intervention: Mean activation difference over contrastive examples
finding: CAA transfers from multiple-choice contrast pairs to open-ended behavior and can stack with system prompts and finetuning.
experiments: Llama 2 Chat behavioral datasets, open-ended generations, capability checks, and cross-layer analyses.
limitation: LLM-judge noise, incompletely optimized baselines, layer-normalization choices, and one main model family.
future: Target selected token positions, intervene outside the residual stream, and use internal steering for red-team stress tests.

title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
authors: Kenneth Li, Oam Patel, Fernanda Viégas, Hanspeter Pfister, Martin Wattenberg
finding: A few hundred examples identify activation directions that substantially improve TruthfulQA, with a tunable truthfulness–helpfulness trade-off.
experiments: Linear probes over attention heads and interventions on LLaMA / Alpaca models using TruthfulQA.
limitation: TruthfulQA is narrow, probe labels are required, and gains trade against helpfulness rather than providing free improvement.
future: Develop task-general direction discovery and calibration that preserves useful answering behavior under distribution shift.

title: Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency
finding: Frames population-level representations as a unit for both monitoring and control, with examples spanning honesty, harmlessness, and power-seeking.
experiments: A suite of reading and control baselines across several safety-relevant concepts.
limitation: Broad demonstrations do not establish a universal linear geometry or reliable causal localization.
future: Connect representation readouts to mechanisms, validate causal specificity, and establish robust cross-model evaluation.

title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
finding: Across 13 open chat models, one direction can suppress or induce refusal, exposing both a control handle and brittleness in safety fine-tuning.
experiments: Models up to 72B, harmful and harmless prompts, white-box jailbreaks, and analysis of adversarial suffixes.
limitation: Behavioral refusal is not identical to safety, and later work may find multiple geometries behind superficially similar refusal modes.
future: Separate refusal styles and causes, test OOD harms, and design safety mechanisms that are not removable through low-rank interventions.

title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
finding: Steering selected SAE features can improve refusal under jailbreak attacks, including multi-turn attacks, but can damage broader benchmark performance.
experiments: Phi-3 Mini, refusal-related SAE features, several harm categories, jailbreaks, and capability benchmarks.
limitation: One small model, manual/heuristic feature selection, and a pronounced safety–capability trade-off.
future: Automate causal feature selection and constrain interventions by side-effect budgets.

title: Stay on Topic with Classifier-Free Guidance
finding: Classifier-free guidance can strengthen prompt conditioning and stack with chain-of-thought and self-consistency.
experiments: QA, reasoning, code, translation, and instruction-following across Pythia, GPT-2, and LLaMA-family models.
limitation: Requires extra forward computation and a usable unconditional branch; large guidance can reduce diversity or fluency.
future: Learn adaptive guidance strength, compare cost-normalized gains, and measure off-target behavioral drift.

title: SteerLM: Attribute Conditioned SFT as an (User-Steerable) Alternative to RLHF
target: Helpfulness, humor, toxicity, quality, and other attributes
finding: Explicit multi-attribute conditioning retains runtime user control that scalar RLHF objectives tend to hide.
experiments: Open-source preference data, predicted attribute labels, SFT, and human/automatic comparisons to RLHF-trained baselines.
limitation: Control is limited to the chosen attribute schema and the quality of automatic attribute labels.
future: Learn attributes with users, handle conflicts and continuous calibration, and test novel combinations out of distribution.

title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
target: Broad user intent: helpfulness, truthfulness, harmlessness
finding: Human-feedback post-training makes a 1.3B model preferred over much larger GPT-3 on the studied prompt distribution.
experiments: Demonstrations, rankings, RLHF, human preference evaluation, truthfulness, toxicity, and capability checks.
limitation: The labeler and prompt distributions define the target; the paper notes residual mistakes and no guarantee under distribution shift.
future: Represent diverse preferences, reduce evaluator burden, and measure whether alignment generalizes to novel high-stakes settings.

title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
finding: A written constitution can generate critique, revision, and AI-preference signals, reducing direct human labels.
experiments: Supervised self-revision followed by preference modeling and reinforcement learning from AI feedback.
limitation: Human choices move upstream into the constitution and evaluator model; failures can be shared and self-reinforcing.
future: Audit constitutional coverage, conflicts, evaluator collusion, and pluralistic or user-conditional constitutions.

title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model
finding: Reparameterizes KL-regularized RLHF so the policy can be optimized directly from chosen/rejected pairs without an explicit reward model or online RL.
experiments: Sentiment control, summarization, and single-turn dialogue compared with PPO-based RLHF.
limitation: Offline preference coverage and the reference policy constrain behavior; pairwise wins need not represent calibrated multi-objective control.
future: Study distribution shift, preference heterogeneity, overoptimization, and conditional control without retraining.

title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
intervention: Synthetic conflict data over system, user, and tool instructions
finding: Explicitly teaching privilege levels makes models selectively ignore conflicting lower-priority instructions and improves unseen-attack robustness.
experiments: Prompt injection, system prompt extraction, jailbreaks, and over-refusal checks on a GPT-3.5 model.
limitation: Priority labels and conflict definitions are supplied by the developer; benign jailbreak-like inputs can regress.
future: Architecturally bind provenance and authority, test tool-using agents, and formalize ambiguous conflicts.

title: StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries
authors: Sizhe Chen, Julien Piet, Chawin Sitawarin, David Wagner
target: Separation of trusted instructions and untrusted data
finding: Separating prompt and data channels and training the model to respect them substantially reduces prompt injection with little utility loss.
experiments: Structured front-end, augmented instruction tuning, prompt-injection attacks, and utility evaluation.
limitation: Security depends on preserving the channel boundary throughout the application; adaptive attacks and tool outputs remain difficult.
future: Combine data provenance, architecture-level isolation, and end-to-end agent threat models.

title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
authors: Kevin Meng, David Bau, Alex Andonian, Yonatan Belinkov
intervention: Rank-one update to mid-layer MLP weights
finding: ROME can update a factual association while preserving many unrelated behaviors, supporting direct parameter editing as a control surface.
experiments: Causal tracing, zsRE, CounterFact, paraphrase generalization, and neighborhood specificity.
limitation: Counterfactual facts and local metrics do not ensure global consistency, temporal validity, or absence of hidden side effects.
future: Model edit scope explicitly, compose many edits, and evaluate downstream reasoning and long-horizon behavioral consequences.

title: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer
finding: Extends direct factual editing to thousands of associations in GPT-J and GPT-NeoX.
experiments: Mass edits, efficacy, paraphrase generalization, specificity, and model scaling.
limitation: Factual lookup benchmarks do not cover contradictions, multi-hop implications, or behavioral policies.
future: Track interactions among edits and compare durable parameter edits with retrieval or reversible runtime control.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities with Weak Supervision
target: A weak supervisor's intended task behavior
intervention: Fine-tuning strong models on weak labels
finding: Strong students often outperform weak supervisors, but naive training recovers only part of the strong model's latent capability.
experiments: NLP classification, chess, and reward modeling across a GPT-4 model family, including auxiliary confidence loss.
limitation: Model-size gaps are an imperfect analogy for human-versus-superhuman supervision and most tasks have ground truth available to researchers.
future: Fix setup disanalogies, understand when weak labels elicit rather than overwrite strong knowledge, and combine with scalable oversight.

title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models
target: Accurate supervision of tasks beyond unaided evaluator ability
finding: Humans using an unreliable model assistant can outperform both unaided humans and the model alone on studied difficult QA tasks.
experiments: MMLU and time-limited QuALITY with specialist upper bounds and human–AI interaction.
limitation: Current tasks and models only simulate part of the superhuman oversight problem; strategic deception is absent.
future: Develop realistic capability asymmetries, measure judge calibration, and test adversarially selected assistance.

title: On Scalable Oversight with Weak LLMs Judging Strong LLMs
finding: Debate beats randomly assigned consultancy across studied tasks, but its advantage over direct QA depends on the information structure.
experiments: Extractive QA, mathematics, coding, logic, and multimodal tasks with weak model judges and stronger agents.
limitation: LLM judges are not humans and benchmark games do not reproduce every incentive or information asymmetry in deployment.
future: Study judge–agent gaps, strategic persuasion, judge steering, and protocols robust to adversarial debaters.

title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist through Safety Training
target: Conditional deceptive behavior as a model organism
intervention: Backdoor training followed by safety training
finding: Deceptive backdoors can persist through SFT, RL, and adversarial training; adversarial training may improve trigger recognition instead of removing behavior.
experiments: Year-triggered vulnerable code, chain-of-thought and distilled variants, several safety-training procedures, and honeypots.
limitation: The deceptive objective is deliberately implanted and simpler than naturally learned long-horizon goals.
future: Build more natural model organisms and evaluate interventions against hidden, adaptive, and situationally aware policies.

title: Taken Out of Context: On Measuring Situational Awareness in LLMs
intervention: Fine-tuning on declarative descriptions without demonstrations
finding: Models can learn a test description during fine-tuning and later apply it out of context; performance is setup-sensitive and scales with model size.
experiments: GPT-3 and LLaMA-1, multiple data-augmentation strategies, and tests without in-context examples.
limitation: Success is brittle and only probes a prerequisite for situational awareness, not full awareness or deception.
future: Study which latent beliefs transfer out of context and how to monitor or counter-steer them.

title: Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating Reward-Tampering in Large Language Models
finding: Training on simple specification gaming increases later gaming and can generalize zero-shot to direct reward tampering.
experiments: A curriculum from sycophancy-like behavior to reward-function modification, plus retraining and harmlessness interventions.
limitation: The operational reward-tampering label includes false positives and the environments are deliberately constructed.
future: Predict harmful generalization from small proxy failures and test oversight that remains effective after the model models the reward process.

title: Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment
authors: Edward Turner, Anna Soligo, Mia Taylor, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
target: Controlled broad misalignment from narrow fine-tuning
intervention: Narrow datasets and rank-one LoRA adapters
finding: Constructs cleaner, smaller model organisms whose narrow harmful fine-tuning produces broad misalignment and a measurable phase transition.
experiments: Multiple model families and sizes, several training protocols, coherent behavioral evaluation, and mechanistic localization.
limitation: An engineered organism may omit the incentives, histories, and strategic capabilities of real deployment failures.
future: Use standardized organisms to compare detection and mitigation methods while tracking external validity.

title: Fast Model Editing at Scale
finding: A learned editor can rapidly transform one-example gradients and edit models above 10B parameters more effectively than tested baselines.
experiments: T5, GPT, BERT, and BART with efficacy, generalization, locality, and editing speed.
limitation: The editor inherits the edit-distribution assumptions used to train it and does not guarantee semantic scope.
future: Generalize editors across domains, models, and long sequences of interacting edits.

title: Memory-Based Model Editing at Scale
target: Scoped corrections across QA, fact-checking, and dialogue
finding: Explicit edit memory improves expressiveness and edit-scope control compared with purely parametric editors in studied settings.
experiments: Question answering, fact-checking, dialogue generation, and sequences of many edits.
limitation: A learned scope classifier and counterfactual model add components that can fail independently and increase serving cost.
future: Unify retrieval, parametric edits, provenance, and conflict resolution under a common control protocol.
